rationale: Aluminium in salt derives from permitted anti-caking additives, not contamination. In the US, sodium aluminosilicate is GRAS as an anti-caking agent in table salt up to 2% (21 CFR 182.2727). In the EU most aluminium-silicate anti-caking additives were removed for consumer protection by Reg (EU) 380/2012 (E556/E558/E559 banned from 2014; E554/E555 restricted to non-salt uses), so EU table salt carries little additive Al. Dietary aluminium is managed by intake against the EFSA TWI (1 mg/kg bw/week) and JECFA PTWI (2 mg/kg bw/week) with additive use-level controls, not by per-food contaminant MLs; oral bioavailability from food is ~0.1-0.3%. No credible regulator sets an aluminium contaminant ML for salt. The single pooled datum (n=1, 164 mg/kg) cannot distinguish additive from natural background.

Older ion-exchange/ETAAS positives are method artifacts. See data/workbench/standards/2026-07-31-chromium-formula-adjudication.md.
regulatory_basis: No Cr-VI ML in any jurisdiction (total-Cr limits e.g. China GB 2762 are total chromium); reference-method non-detection (Cr-VI reduces to Cr-III)
jurisdictions_checked: EU 2023/915; Codex; FDA; AU/NZ Sch 19; China GB 2762-2022
cross_sourced: reference-method adjudication (hernandez2019 68-brand milk/dairy/cereal + saraiva2021) + credible-ML register checked 2026-08-10

rationale: Total chromium in the cereal/grain matrix is dominated by nutritionally-essential Cr(III); Cr(VI) reduces to Cr(III) in the acidic, organic-rich matrix. Firm control: reflex speciation - any total-Cr result >= 100 ug/kg triggers Cr(VI) speciation (EN 15192 / EPA 6800), and any quantifiable Cr(VI) fails; Cr(VI) is never a panel number.
regulatory_basis: No regulatory Cr / Cr(VI) ML for grain/cereal products in any jurisdiction (China GB 2762 regulates total Cr for a few matrices, none of them grains).

rationale: No government sets a methylmercury ML for any grain, cereal, or rice product in any jurisdiction; methylmercury maximum levels exist only for fish and seafood. Mercury in this matrix is controlled by the total-mercury ML (30 ug/kg, Israel FCS-2016), which bounds the methylmercury fraction. Rice can accumulate trace methylmercury via paddy-soil methylation in point-source-contaminated growing regions, but that fraction is bounded by the total-mercury control and no methylmercury ML exists to look up.

rationale: No government sets a total-chromium or hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any legume, pulse, peanut, or soy product in any jurisdiction. Chromium in this plant matrix is dominated by nutritionally-essential Cr(III), and Cr(VI) reduces to Cr(III) in the organic-rich matrix. Firm control: reflex speciation - any total-Cr result >= 100 ug/kg triggers Cr(VI) speciation, and any quantifiable Cr(VI) fails; Cr(VI) is never a panel number.
regulatory_basis: No regulatory total-Cr or Cr(VI) ML for legume/pulse/peanut/soy products in any jurisdiction; the only register total-Cr MLs are for dairy powder, drinking water, and fertiliser.

rationale: Every government tin maximum level in the register is scoped to canned / tin-coated product; tin migrates from tinplate, and that packaging-migration pathway is the contamination these MLs regulate. Dried legumes, pulses, peanuts, peanut butter, and soy products are not sold in tinplate, so that pathway is absent. Routed occurrence that has screened tin in these matrices reports it at or near non-detect (Roman-Ochoa 2021 measured bean tin at ~0.00 mg/kg against a sub-ppb LOD), i.e. dietary background rather than tinplate migration. Canned legume/pea products route to the canned-foods category and carry the tin ML there.
regulatory_basis: Tin MLs (EU/UK/GSO/IN 50000+ ug/kg; IN canned green peas / canned mushrooms) apply to canned product only; no non-canned legume/pulse Sn ML exists in any jurisdiction.
